newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir commander unwell ahead of risky repair job.
newsitem.headline: Mir commander unwell ahead of risky repair job.

text.p: The Russian commander of the crippled Mir space station is overtired and has a problem with his cardiovascular system, Mission Control said on Monday.

Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, who is due to undertake risky repairs at the end of the week to save the ageing station, said he had noticed the trouble shortly after the remote-controlled cargo craft he was manoeuvring slammed into Mir on June 25.
"It came as a surprise," he said during a crackly television link-up with Mission Control at Korolyov, outside Moscow.
Journalists could not hear his description of the trouble due to static. Experts on the ground called it a cardiovascular problem -- relating to the heart, blood supply or lungs,
Tsibliyev asked whether he could take any medicine, but was advised against it before he and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin enter Mir's damaged Spektr module for the repairs.
Their American colleague, NASA physicist Michael Foale, will sit in the escape capsule to evacuate all three if something goes wrong during the complex and unprecedented operation.
"The main thing is not to worry. I cannot recommend any medicine for you. Try to rest as much as possible," a Mission Control doctor told Tsibliyev.

"Today we have carried out medical experiments using an exercise bike to test the cosmonauts' cardiovascular systems...Tsibliyev's reaction appeared to be negative," Mission Control spokesman Valery Lyndin said after the television linkup.
"The doctors' initial reaction is that Tsibliyev is overtired. He has problems with his sleep but his general condition is within the norm".

Spektr was holed during the collision -- Mir's worst ever accident -- and, airless, it is now sealed off from the station. Tsibliyev and Lazutkin are due to undertake the complex repair works on Thursday or Friday night.

Mission Control transmitted a video of a mock-up of the unprecedented repair operation undertaken by fellow cosmonauts wearing bulky space suits in a swimming pool -- the nearest they could get to conditions in orbit.
It will be studied by the crew before a planned six-hour dress rehearsal on the cramped 11-year-old station on Tuesday.
British-born Foale will be on hand to help his Russian colleagues during the trial run. The job will be on Thursday or Friday night, mission director Vladimir Solovyov said.
The two cosmonauts have prepared their spacesuits for the sortie into the holed Spektr module to reconnect electric cables and restore power from the module's solar panels.
Rapid reactions after the collision allowed the crew to seal off the Spektr as air escaped through the hole. But closing the hatches meant cutting off up to half of Mir's power supply.

A Progress cargo vessel brought repair tools and other vital supplies to Mir a week ago and the crew have now finished unloading it. Among the supplies was equipment to improve communications, making it easier for the cosmonauts to view the training film and stay in contact with Earth during the repairs.
But the crew have been puzzling over the purpose of one bit of equipment they found on Progress.

"We are trying to get an answer from you, what is that tap which looks like one in the kitchen? Tsiblieyev said in Monday's television exchange. But no one could immediately tell him. "Wait and we will find out," replied a Mission Control official.
